summary:
Oman criminalises same-sex conduct under the 2018 Penal Law, with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment. The law applies to both men and women, and suspects may be prosecuted without a prior complaint where the act causes a public scandal. A trans visitor in a relationship that local law would class as same-sex falls within the same exposure. The same statute set reaches gender expression and presentation, and the offences are enforced against foreign nationals.

Article 265 of the Penal Law (Royal Decree 7/2018) covers public indecency, punishable by 10 days to 3 months' imprisonment and a fine of OMR 100 to 300. Article 266 covers impersonation and entering women-only venues while disguised, carrying 1 month to 1 year; Article 266(d) is the route through which gender non-conformity is punished. Articles 267 and 268 cover producing or sharing content judged to violate public morals, offline and online, with penalties of up to 1 year and 10 days to 1 month respectively. The Cyber Crime Law 2011, Articles 17 and 31, has been used against LGBT expression, carrying 1 month to 3 years and fines of OMR 100 to 3,000. The 2018 code added the provision punishing any man who appears to dress in women's clothing.

The Public Prosecution has stated that any male who appears in female clothing or demeanour may be fined up to OMR 3,000 and jailed for up to one year, with additional charges available for publishing such material on social media.

Enforcement is documented. In September 2018 a Salalah preliminary court sentenced two men to four years' imprisonment and fined them OMR 3,000 each for cross-dressing and sharing photographs of themselves in women's clothing on social media, and two further men to three years with the same fine for appearing in the video. The Royal Oman Police had arrested a group of men in January 2018 for dressing as women after social-media photographs circulated. In July 2020 Human Rights Watch wrote to the authorities about arrests and convictions under the imitating-the-opposite-sex provision, including arrests announced by the Royal Oman Police of men in women's clothing after photographs from a private party in Salalah circulated, and the case of an Asian expatriate detained in an abaya and niqab during a women-only park hour in Al Buraimi.

Border and airport screening carries a direct risk of outing and mistreatment. A genderqueer, non-binary Indian model and activist arriving at Muscat International Airport on a 10-day tourist visa in February 2023 said her friends cleared immigration while she was held for a separate examination, made to remove her shirt and touched inappropriately by officers.

Foreign nationals face an additional consequence. Article 60 requires deportation for a foreign national convicted of a felony, permanently, and permits it for a misdemeanour for 3 to 15 years.

Prosecution is often triggered by digital evidence found during unrelated investigations rather than by a family complaint; Article 49 provides a dual-criminality exception. The state internet service provider, Omantel, enables surveillance. Outing therefore carries both social and criminal risk.

Legal gender recognition is not available, and gender-affirming healthcare is explicitly banned. A joint stakeholder submission by Cairo 52 and White Tent to Oman's fourth-cycle UN Universal Periodic Review in August 2025 documents systemic legal and institutional discrimination against transgender people, states that recent legislative developments have deepened the criminalisation of gender expression, and records that Oman has not acted on earlier UPR recommendations on gender identity, expression and health access. The submission recommends ending criminalisation, adopting anti-discrimination legislation and permitting legal recognition.

Assembly and advocacy are restricted through the Civil Associations Law, and advocacy for LGBT rights is treated as a criminal act.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch's 2018 regional report places Oman's cross-dressing provision alongside Kuwait's 2007 imitation law, indicating that the offence type is shared across the subregion rather than unique to Oman.

In September 2013 the Gulf Cooperative Countries discussed a proposal to devise a test for homosexuality intended to single out gay foreigners and prevent them from entering member states. Officials described it as a mere proposal and the discussion was not carried forward, with concern over hosting the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar cited as a reason for backtracking. No such screening is in force.
localsOnly:
Residents have no route to legal gender recognition, and gender-affirming healthcare is explicitly banned.

Advocacy for LGBT rights is a criminal act. Activists operate through social media under aliases to protect their identities, with very rare exceptions, and formal organising is restricted by the Civil Associations Law.

Oman has not implemented earlier Universal Periodic Review recommendations on gender identity, gender expression and access to health services.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Dignity Trust country profile for Oman could not be retrieved at research time (HTTP 403). Its documented content on the criminalisation of same-sex activity and gender expression could not be verified directly against the source.

Sources give inconsistent article numbering for the relevant provisions. The cross-dressing offence is cited as Article 22 in one report and as Article 266 in the statute extraction; the same-sex conduct provisions are cited as sections 33 and 223. The numbering is unresolved.

No source states where inside the prison system gender-nonconforming people convicted in Oman were housed.

No source provides a documented statement on societal tolerance of transgender people specifically in Oman; the available material addresses LGBT populations generally.

A scholarly source on religious and legal frameworks distinguishes criminalisation of homosexual acts from criminalisation of identity in some jurisdictions, but offers no Oman-specific finding and is not relied on here.
